credit.credit-words: Just Intonation
A bit of theory
BH
Background - The Harmonic Series
When a string or a column of air vibrates, it does so in incrementing fractions of it's length: 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 etc.
These additional frequencies are variously called overtones, partials or harmonics and the particular mix of
overtones and the way that mix develops over time is what gives an instrument its timbre.
The entire (infinite) set of these frequencies is called the harmonic series.
The lowest, whole string vibration in this series is called the fundamental.
The first harmonic (1/2) vibrates at twice the frequency of the fundamental and sounds an octave higher.
The second harmonic (1/3) vibrates at three times the frequency of the fundamental and sounds an octave
plus a perfect fifth higher.
The third (1/4) is two octaves higher.
The fourth (1/5) sounds two octaves plus a major third higher.
Etc.
Now you may think that you could use the harmonic series to generate all of the notes of the western scale, but
in fact the upper harmonics sound very out of tune to our ears.
On the other hand the major and minor thirds, perfect fourth and perfect fifth low in the series sound very
pure, because of their simple frequency ratios.
Though that Major third might sound a bit spicy to our modern ears, there are reasons for that which we'll cover
in a bit.
Background - The Cycle of Fifths
Keys in western music differ in the number of sharps or flats they contain. Ignoring minor keys for now, the
most closely related keys differ by only one sharp or flat, for example F (one flat) and C, or G (one sharp) and
D (two sharps.) These most closely related keys are a fifth apart, and so it is possible to arrange all 12 major (or
minor) keys in a big circle with adjacent keys a fifth apart:
Then the distance between two keys becomes immediately visible, for example the most remotely related pairs
of keys are opposite one another in this cycle. Moving clockwise adds sharps or removes flats. Moving counter-
clockwise adds flats or removes sharps.
Tuning in Fifths
One alternative way to make a scale then would be to tune in fifths. The second harmonic is an octave and a fifth
above the fundamental, and if we divide that frequency by two (tune down an octave) we get a note that vibrates
at 3/2 times the fundamental and sounds a perfect fifth above. For example starting with C we get G.
We take that new note as our new fundamental and repeat the process, so continuing our example, from G we get
to D. Continuing we eventually generate all of the notes of the chromatic scale.
This is called Pythagorean Tuning:
(I've kept all the notes within one octave to save on ledger lines but it doesn't affect the concept.)
Thinking about it, it was clear that this wasn't going to work, because to get the next frequency, you multiply
the previous one by 3/2:
and so on generating increasingly complex fractions that obviously never return to 1.
The Modern Solution - Equal Temperament
The solution to this problem nowadays is to slightly flatten each of those fifths, by approximately 2% of a
semitone each, so that we do arrive back on the C we started from. This is called "Equal Temperament" (ET).
"Equal" because all of the fifths are the same width, and "Temperament" because we are "tempering" (adjusting)
the intervals.
This sounds like a great idea, and in fact all modern western instruments are tuned using ET, but it has some
drawbacks which I'll get to. Before that though, we need a little more terminology.
Terminology - Cents
A cent is defined as 1/100th of an equal tempered semitone. It is simpler to use than ratios: because it is a
logarithmic scale we can simply add and subtract cents rather than having to multiply and divide ratios.
If you're curious the formula is
cents = log
(ratio)
Cents are a relative measure, they are normally used to describe differences from equal temperament. However
if we arbitrarily describe middle C (C4) as being at 0 cents, then in Equal Temperament C♯4 is 100, D4 is 200,
E♭4 is 300 etc, all the way to C5 at 1200.
The difference of 1 cent is inaudible, even to a trained ear. The smallest interval a trained ear can hear is
probably around 8 to 10 cents, see how you do:
By the way, if you click on a note in MuseScore and look at the "Tuning" value in the inspector, that value is in
cents, and represents the difference from equal tempered pitch.
Terminology - Commas
A comma is a value, usually given in cents, that describes the discrepancy between the pitch of the same note
tuned in different ways. There are two commas we need to know about:
The Ditonic Comma
is the difference between that B♯ we arrived at by tuning in pure fifths and the C
that we started on. It's almost exactly 24 cents, hence ET flattens each fifth by 2 cents.
The Syntonic Comma
is even more egregious, it's the difference between the major third we get from
Pythagorean Tuning and the fourth harmonic. It is around 22 cents. Even though ET flattens major thirds by
cents (C-G-D-A-E = 4 fifths) that still means the pure major third is 14 cents flatter than the ET
one. In the example below we subtract 14 cents from the ET 3rd to get the pure harmonic third, and we add 2
cents to the ET fifth to get a pure 5th. The difference between a pure major triad and an ET one is quite audible.
This is the first of the problems with Equal Temperament: it's out of tune, but we've just gotten used to it.
There are other problems with it too, because of how it compares with other approaches. There are a host of
alternatives to ET, which rely on distributing the ditonic comma around the circle of fifths in different ways.
Some of these alternative temperaments are
irregular
, meaning they have no repeating pattern. These irregular
temperaments result in each key having a slightly different character or feel, in which context statements
musicians have made about i.e. E major being "bright" or F major being "pastoral" make a lot more sense. Many
people argue that music lost a lot of it's colour with the adoption of ET, because now keys differ only in pitch.
An interesting digression: it was often asserted in the past that Bach wrote his "Well-tempered Clavier"
(two books of 24 preludes and fugues in each of the major and minor keys) in order to promote Equal
Temperament, but in a great piece of detective work one Bradley Lehmann demonstrated (at least he
convinces me) that not only was Bach promoting his own individual irregular temperament, but that he
left instructions on how to tune it hidden in plain sight on the front cover of the first edition of the WTC!
Google for Bach Tuning or Bradley Lehmann if you're interested in following that story.
Just Intonation, finally
With all of that behind us we're at last in a position to discuss the other alternative to equal temperament,
Just intonation. In its simplest form it is represented by the following diagram, or variations on it, called
"Warpurg's Monochord no. 1" (a Monochord was a mediaeval single stringed instrument used to experiment
with pitch, I presume the diagram was derived using one.)
It's a bit intimidating at first, but if you study it you can see that:
It contains all 12 notes of the chromatic scale.
Horizontal lines connect notes a perfect fifth apart (A, E, B etc.)
Diagonal lines going bottom left to top right connect notes a major third apart (F, A C♯ etc.)
Diagonal lines going top left to bottom right connect notes a minor third apart (A, C, E♭ etc.)
Because of the above:
Upward pointing triangles all denote major triads (C, E, G etc.)
Downward pointing triangles denote minor triads (C, E♭ G etc.)
Not all triads are represented, for example there is no triangle for D Minor (D, F, A).
Now it turns out to be possible to tune all 12 notes so that all of the fifths and thirds that are directly connected
on this diagram are pure, according to the harmonic series.
The boxes contain the requisite offsets from ET in cents to achieve this, starting with the arbitrary decision to
make C zero: Major thirds are narrowed by 14 cents and perfect fifths are widened by 2 cents, just as in our
previous example.
In more detail, since C is 0, G must be sharpened 2 cents, since G is now 2, D must be sharpened by 4 cents
and so on. Similarily since C is 0, E must be flattened by 14 cents, and since we already know G is 2, we now
know the amount to temper minor thirds by: +16 cents. So for example we need to sharpen B♭ by 18 (2 + 16).
Continuing in this way we can calculate all of the note offsets, without conflict.
Nonetheless, as long as we stick to triads that are dignified by occupying a triangle in the monochord, we can
have perfect harmony:
Or almost perfect, that passing 6/4 D minor marked with a "*" doesn't fit in our monochord. There are a number
of ways to address this, discussed next.
First of all, here's that diagram again, with more additions.
The additional notes are merely repetitions of the notes we have already and in fact we can extend the diagram
arbitrarily in all directions.
The first approach is to slide the central monochord around in this space. For example moving one to the right
would replace F with C, A with E etc., while the cent offsets move with it, so G gets 0, effectively a rotation
one step clockwise around the circle of fifths. The idea then is to try to find a location for the monochord that
does encompass all of the triads we are using. This can work, but for our particular problem it doesn't seem to,
for example in moving one to the right we would gain a D minor triad, but loose F Major.
Another approach is to change the shape of the monochord, for example instead of the F at the bottom left we
could instead choose the F at centre top or bottom right. Of course these have to be re-tuned to maintain pure
intervals (F at centre top would be -44 for example.)
The last approach is what is getting just intonation a lot of attention recently, it is more properly called
Dynamic Temperament, and it gets a section to itself.
The idea is that rather than sliding the monochord around the grid or changing its shape, we can just extend the
monochord by continuing to tune in perfect intervals. So to get our D minor triad, we notice we already have
F and A connected on the left with D greyed out to the left of those. If we continue the pattern of cent values, we
get a D with offset -18. This D is not the same as the one we have already, it's a very noticeable 22 cents lower.
Obviously this approach won't work for fixed pitch instruments, but for voices, or any instrument where the
performer has precise control over pitch, it's possible.
However in our case it's still not right because we're already holding over a D from the previous chord and so we
instead need to tune a new A (+6) and F (+20) from the D on the right. Finally we have pure harmony.
Admittedly it sounds a bit odd on a piano where you're not expecting to hear the same note with different tunings!
Dynamic Temperament
Many perfomers, noteably string quartets and barbershop quartets gravitate towards just intonation wherever
possible because it just sounds better. However the potential for tonal drift (wandering off the edge of the
monochord) has, in the past, curtailed this practice. Plus, when singing with accompaniment by fixed pitch
instruments Just Intonation can sound a little off.
More recently though, composers and performers have started to actively exploit this tonal drift. Famously
Jacob Collier who spectacularly modulates to G half sharp in his piece "In the Bleak Midwinter".
By considering Dynamic Temperament as described, it's possible to start to understand how he did it.
While I'm not going to repeat that feat, let's at least try a little experiment along the same lines to conclude.
Using a chromatic mediant progression in minor thirds: C, E♭, F♯, A C, we'll move down and right through the
monochord to arrive back at a very different C from the one we started on - 64 cents sharp, keeping common
notes between chords at the same pitch. If you're confused, just follow the triangles for each chord beginning on
C, E, G.
Modern Approaches to Dynamic Temperament
One last point worth mentioning is that Dynamic Temperament applies to any technique that uses different
tunings for the same notes within a single piece, it's not limited to Just Intonation but since Just Intonation is the
holy grail of tuning it is often the target of Dynamic Temperament.
